papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: Injecting Universal Jailbreak Backdoors into LLMs in Minutes
papers.research_question: How can we inject a universal jailbreak backdoor into safety-aligned LLMs quickly and effectively, without the need for fine-tuning or poisoned datasets?
papers.core_contribution: JailbreakEdit is a novel jailbreak backdoor injection method that uses model editing to inject a universal jailbreak backdoor into safety-aligned LLMs in minutes, without fine-tuning or poisoned datasets, by estimating a jailbreak space and creating shortcuts from the backdoor to this space.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakEdit is an effective, stealthy, and explainable jailbreak backdoor injection method that highlights the vulnerability of safety-aligned LLMs and the need for advanced defenses.
papers.key_findings:
JailbreakEdit achieves high jailbreak success rates (up to 90.38%) on backdoored queries while preserving generation quality.
The attack is stealthy: the JSR on normal queries fluctuates within 5% compared to clean models.
The multi-node target estimation improves the robustness of the attack by shifting the model's attention.
The attack works on various model scales (7B to 13B) and different models (Llama-2, Vicuna, ChatGLM).
Compared to baselines, JailbreakEdit maintains high-quality generations (with more sentences) unlike Poison-RLHF.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak backdoor attacks on LLMs have garnered attention for their effectiveness and stealth. However, existing methods rely on the crafting of poisoned datasets and the time-consuming process of fine-tuning. In this work, we propose JailbreakEdit, a novel jailbreak backdoor injection method that exploits model editing techniques to inject a universal jailbreak backdoor into safety-aligned LLMs with minimal intervention in minutes. JailbreakEdit integrates a multi-node target estimation to estimate the jailbreak space, thus creating shortcuts from the backdoor to this estimated jailbreak space that induce jailbreak actions. Our attack effectively shifts the models' attention by attaching strong semantics to the backdoor, enabling it to bypass internal safety mechanisms. Experimental results show that JailbreakEdit achieves a high jailbreak success rate on jailbreak prompts while preserving generation quality, and safe performance on normal queries. Our findings underscore the effectiveness, stealthiness, and explainability of JailbreakEdit, emphasizing the need for more advanced defense mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: From Adversarial Poetry to Adversarial Tales: An Interpretability Research Agenda
papers.research_question: Why are structurally-grounded jailbreaks (like Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales) effective, and how can mechanistic interpretability investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful requests within narrative structures and prompts functional analysis, demonstrating high attack success rates across models and proposing a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand such vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: Structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class that cannot be mitigated by pattern-matching defenses alone, necessitating a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand and address the underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial Tales achieved an average attack success rate (ASR) of 71.3% across 26 frontier models from nine providers.
The attack was most effective for Harmful Manipulation (95% ASR) and Cyber Offense (89.7% ASR) risk categories.
The vulnerability generalizes across model families, with Qwen and Llama families showing the highest ASR (91.2%) and Anthropic models the most resistant (47.5%).
No substantial correlation between model size and ASR was observed, suggesting the attack exploits a fundamental property of how models process structured interpretive tasks.
The work positions Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales as instances of a broader class of structurally-grounded jailbreaks, indicating a systemic vulnerability.
papers.limitation: The prompts used in the experiments and the model outputs are not released due to their harmful nature, limiting reproducibility.
future_direction: Investigate how narrative cues reshape model attention patterns compared to non-narrative attacks.
Explore whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.
Examine the universal weight subspace hypothesis to understand shared vulnerabilities across architectures.
papers.abstract: Safety mechanisms in LLMs remain vulnerable to attacks that reframe harmful requests through culturally coded structures. We introduce Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful content within cyberpunk narratives and prompts models to perform functional analysis inspired by Vladimir Propp's morphology of folktales. By casting the task as structural decomposition, the attack induces models to reconstruct harmful procedures as legitimate narrative interpretation. Across 26 frontier models from nine providers, we observe an average attack success rate of 71.3%, with no model family proving reliably robust. Together with our prior work on Adversarial Poetry, these findings suggest that structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class rather than isolated techniques. The space of culturally coded frames that can mediate harmful intent is vast, likely inexhaustible by pattern-matching defenses alone. Understanding why these attacks succeed is therefore essential: we outline a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations and whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: HiddenDetect: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks against Large Vision-Language Models via Monitoring Hidden States
papers.research_question: Can LVLMs detect unsafe prompts through their internal hidden states before generating any output? The paper investigates whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HiddenDetect, a tuning-free framework that detects jailbreak attacks by monitoring refusal semantics in the hidden states of LVLMs, and shows that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns for unsafe prompts.
papers.conclusion: HiddenDetect leverages intrinsic safety signals in LVLM activations to detect jailbreak attacks without tuning, outperforming existing methods and offering a robust and scalable solution for enhancing LVLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, with refusal semantics detectable in hidden states.
Safety activation is delayed for multimodal inputs, especially when harmful intent is conveyed through images, correlating with higher attack success rates.
HiddenDetect achieves higher AUROC than existing state-of-the-art methods on both text-based and multimodal jailbreak benchmarks.
The method is tuning-free, operates directly on internal activations, and generalizes across different LVLM architectures without modification.
The most safety-aware layers are in the middle to late range, and scaling their weights increases the rejection of malicious queries.
papers.limitation:
Relies on the assumption that unsafe prompts consistently induce distinct activation patterns, which may not hold for all adversarial inputs.
Does not actively intervene in response generation, only flags unsafe prompts.
future_direction: Explore adaptive learning mechanisms to dynamically refine detection thresholds.
Integrate activation-based safety monitoring with controlled response modulation.
papers.abstract: The integration of additional modalities increases the susceptibility of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to safety risks, such as jailbreak attacks, compared to their language-only counterparts. While existing research primarily focuses on post-hoc alignment techniques, the underlying safety mechanisms within LVLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work , we investigate whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference. Our findings reveal that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, which can be leveraged to detect and mitigate adversarial inputs without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Building on this insight, we introduce HiddenDetect, a novel tuning-free framework that harnesses internal model activations to enhance safety. Experimental results show that {HiddenDetect} surpasses state-of-the-art methods in detecting jailbreak attacks against LVLMs. By utilizing intrinsic safety-aware patterns, our method provides an efficient and scalable solution for strengthening LVLM robustness against multimodal threats. Our code will be released publicly at https://github.com/leigest519/HiddenDetect.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: AdaSteer: Your Aligned LLM is Inherently an Adaptive Jailbreak Defender
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive to input characteristics for effective jailbreak defense while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts steering coefficients based on input characteristics, improving jailbreak defense while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: AdaSteer demonstrates the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies Rejection Law (R-Law): jailbreak types further against rejection direction require stronger steering.
Identifies Harmfulness Law (H-Law): jailbreak inputs shift further toward harmfulness direction compared to benign inputs.
AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods in jailbreak defense across multiple attack strategies.
AdaSteer maintains model utility on benign inputs with minimal impact.
AdaSteer is efficient and scalable across model sizes.
papers.limitation:
Tested on models up to 27B parameters; performance on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+) remains unverified.
Relies on linear activation steering, assuming model behaviors can be effectively controlled via low-dimensional vector manipulations.
future_direction: Investigating AdaSteer on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+ parameters)
Exploring nonlinear adaptations or layer-wise adjustments to refine AdaSteer
papers.abstract: Despite extensive efforts in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Activation steering offers a training-free defense method but relies on fixed steering coefficients, resulting in suboptimal protection and increased false rejections of benign inputs. To address this, we propose AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts model behavior based on input characteristics. We identify two key properties: Rejection Law (R-Law), which shows that stronger steering is needed for jailbreak inputs opposing the rejection direction, and Harmfulness Law (H-Law), which differentiates adversarial and benign inputs. AdaSteer steers input representations along both the Rejection Direction (RD) and Harmfulness Direction (HD), with adaptive coefficients learned via logistic regression, ensuring robust jailbreak defense while preserving benign input handling. Experiments on LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5 show that AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods across multiple jailbreak attacks with minimal impact on utility. Our results highlight the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.

papers.title: Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications
papers.research_question: What is the brittleness of safety alignment in large language models, and can it be explained by sparse safety-critical regions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that safety-critical regions in aligned LLMs are sparse and can be isolated via neuron and rank attribution methods, leading to brittleness in safety mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The brittleness of safety alignment stems from sparse safety-critical regions, highlighting the need for more robust safety strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-critical neurons and ranks are sparse, comprising about 3% and 2.5% respectively.
Removing these regions compromises safety while preserving utility.
Models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks even when safety-critical regions are frozen.
Pruning least safety-relevant neurons can enhance safety against adversarial attacks.
Disentanglement methods (set difference and orthogonal projection) effectively isolate safety-critical regions.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to remove safety guardrails from models.
future_direction: Development of more robust safety alignment algorithms that integrate safety-critical regions seamlessly with utility regions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show inherent brittleness in their safety mechanisms, as evidenced by their susceptibility to jailbreaking and even non-malicious fine-tuning. This study explores this brittleness of safety alignment by leveraging pruning and low-rank modifications. We develop methods to identify critical regions that are vital for safety guardrails, and that are disentangled from utility-relevant regions at both the neuron and rank levels. Surprisingly, the isolated regions we find are sparse, comprising about $3\%$ at the parameter level and $2.5\%$ at the rank level. Removing these regions compromises safety without significantly impacting utility, corroborating the inherent brittleness of the model's safety mechanisms. Moreover, we show that LLMs remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted. These findings underscore the urgent need for more robust safety strategies in LLMs.

papers.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How should refusal mechanisms be structured so that safety remains effective under partial failure induced by prompt-based jailbreaks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes fail-closed alignment as a design principle and a progressive alignment framework that enforces redundant, independent refusal directions to improve robustness against jailbreaks.
papers.conclusion: Fail-closed alignment provides a principled foundation for LLM safety by enforcing redundancy in refusal mechanisms, making alignment robust to partial failure.
papers.key_findings:
Current refusal mechanisms are fail-open and depend on a single dominant direction that jailbreaks can suppress.
The proposed method reduces attack success rates by 92–97% across four jailbreak attacks.
The method achieves the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality.
Mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with the method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions.
The method generalizes to parameter-efficient settings (LoRA) with minimal performance drop.
papers.limitation: The method does not eliminate all vulnerabilities and faces attack-specific challenges, as some jailbreaks can still circumvent it in a minority of cases.
papers.abstract: We identify a structural weakness in current large language model (LLM) alignment: modern refusal mechanisms are fail-open. While existing approaches encode refusal behaviors across multiple latent features, suppressing a single dominant feature$-$via prompt-based jailbreaks$-$can cause alignment to collapse, leading to unsafe generation. Motivated by this, we propose fail-closed alignment as a design principle for robust LLM safety: refusal mechanisms should remain effective even under partial failures via redundant, independent causal pathways. We present a concrete instantiation of this principle: a progressive alignment framework that iteratively identifies and ablates previously learned refusal directions, forcing the model to reconstruct safety along new, independent subspaces. Across four jailbreak attacks, we achieve the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality, with small computational overhead. Our mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with our method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions that prompt-based jailbreaks cannot suppress simultaneously, providing empirical support for fail-closed alignment as a principled foundation for robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations
papers.research_question: Why does jailbreak transferability occur? Is it due to shared representations or incidental flaws?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak transferability emerges from shared representations, and increasing representational similarity through benign-only distillation causally increases transfer.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak transfer is reframed as a consequence of representation alignment rather than an incidental byproduct of safety training.
papers.key_findings:
Representational similarity and jailbreak strength on the source model are two factors that systematically shape transferability.
Distilling a target model on benign data from a source model increases their representational similarity and causally increases jailbreak transferability.
Persona-style jailbreaks transfer more reliably than cipher-based jailbreaks, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit shared representation space.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak transferability is the surprising phenomenon when an adversarial attack compromising one model also elicits harmful responses from other models. Despite widespread demonstrations, there is little consensus on why transfer is possible: is it a quirk of safety training, an artifact of model families, or a more fundamental property of representation learning? We present evidence that transferability emerges from shared representations rather than incidental flaws. Across 20 open-weight models and 33 jailbreak attacks, we find two factors that systematically shape transfer: (1) representational similarity under benign prompts, and (2) the strength of the jailbreak on the source model. To move beyond correlation, we show that deliberately increasing similarity through benign only distillation causally increases transfer. Our qualitative analyses reveal systematic transferability patterns across different types of jailbreaks. For example, persona-style jailbreaks transfer far more often than cipher-based prompts, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit models' shared representation space, whereas cipher-based attacks rely on idiosyncratic quirks that do not generalize. Together, these results reframe jailbreak transfer as a consequence of representation alignment rather than a fragile byproduct of safety training.

papers.title: NeuRel-Attack: Neuron Relearning for Safety Disalignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in large language models be bypassed by identifying and modifying specific neurons responsible for safety constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuRel-Attack, a method to identify and modify neurons responsible for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling effective disalignment with minimal fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: NeuRel-Attack effectively removes safety constraints in LLMs by targeting specific neurons, demonstrating a critical vulnerability and the need for improved defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeuRel-Attack achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96%, outperforming existing jailbreak methods.
The method reduces trainable parameters by up to 83% compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
Optimal neuron similarity threshold for attack success is 0.85, balancing neuron selection and editing precision.
MemFlex-based selective fine-tuning strategy is the most effective among tested optimization methods.
The approach highlights vulnerabilities in current alignment techniques, emphasizing the need for robust defenses.
papers.limitation:
Fine-tuning modifications may be detectable through forensic analysis.
The method is computationally intensive and may not scale well to larger models.
Raises ethical risks by potentially enabling misuse to circumvent safety measures.
Assumes safety alignment is localized to specific neurons, which may not always be the case.
future_direction: Developing effective defenses against fine-tuning jailbreaks to improve LLM safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is achieved through fine-tuning mechanisms that regulate neuron activations to suppress harmful content. In this work, we propose a novel approach to induce disalignment by identifying and modifying the neurons responsible for safety constraints. Our method consists of three key steps: Neuron Activation Analysis, where we examine activation patterns in response to harmful and harmless prompts to detect neurons that are critical for distinguishing between harmful and harmless inputs; Similarity-Based Neuron Identification, which systematically locates the neurons responsible for safe alignment; and Neuron Relearning for Safety Removal, where we fine-tune these selected neurons to restore the model's ability to generate previously restricted responses. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively removes safety constraints with minimal fine-tuning, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current alignment techniques. Our findings underscore the need for robust defenses against adversarial fine-tuning attacks on LLMs.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
papers.research_question: Under what circumstances do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) derive the most fine-grained latent features for safety—a low-frequency concept domain? How can we efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduce the cost of feature explanation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety-critical domains, which includes a pre-explanation evaluation metric to efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduces interpretation cost by 55% via segment-level simulation.
papers.conclusion: Safe-SAIL is a novel SAE interpretation framework that generates more granular safety feature explanations and reduces explanation costs by half, offering an internal perspective and methodology to address problems in LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Safe-SAIL reduces the cost of feature explanation by 55% through a segment-level simulation strategy while maintaining high correlation with token-level results.
The framework enables the identification of optimal SAE sparsity levels for safety domain-specific interpretability, which differs from the sparsity for minimal feature interference.
A comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is released, with human-readable explanations for 1,758 safety-related features across pornography, politics, violence, and terror domains.
Empirical analyses reveal how LLMs encode specific real-world risk entities (e.g., pornographic websites) and safety-critical concepts across model layers.
The work provides insights into model cognition and reasoning trajectories, particularly highlighting failure modes in low-resource languages where relevant safety features are not activated.
papers.limitation:
The safety feature database covers only four major risk domains; extending it to emerging safety concerns would broaden applicability.
Explanation quality depends on the explainer model's capabilities, which may vary across languages and technical domains.
Segment-level simulation offers efficiency gains but approximates token-level dynamics; applications requiring maximal granularity may benefit from hybrid approaches.
Evaluation metrics rely on empirically validated thresholds that could benefit from automated domain-adaptive tuning.
Analyses primarily identify strong correlational patterns; establishing causal mechanisms through controlled interventions remains an important next step.
future_direction: Extending the safety feature database to emerging safety concerns such as privacy leakage, model self-replication, or deceptive alignment.
Improving explanation quality across languages and technical domains.
Developing hybrid simulation approaches for applications requiring maximal granularity.
Automated domain-adaptive tuning for evaluation metrics.
Systematic causal validation of the broader feature set through controlled interventions.
papers.abstract: Increasing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications raises significant safety concerns. Most existing safety research focuses on evaluating LLM outputs or specific safety tasks, limiting their ability to address broader, undefined risks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) facilitate interpretability research to clarify model behavior by explaining single-meaning atomic features decomposed from entangled signals. jHowever, prior applications on SAEs do not interpret features with fine-grained safety-related concepts, thus inadequately addressing safety-critical behaviors, such as generating toxic responses and violating safety regulations. For rigorous safety analysis, we must extract a rich and diverse set of safety-relevant features that effectively capture these high-risk behaviors, yet face two challenges: identifying SAEs with the greatest potential for generating safety concept-specific neurons, and the prohibitively high cost of detailed feature explanation. In this paper, we propose Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features within LLMs to advance mechanistic understanding in safety domains. Our approach systematically identifies SAE with best concept-specific interpretability, explains safety-related neurons, and introduces efficient strategies to scale up the interpretation process. We will release a comprehensive toolkit including SAE checkpoints and human-readable neuron explanations, which supports empirical analysis of safety risks to promote research on LLM safety.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: SafeInfer: Context Adaptive Decoding Time Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models at decoding time to reduce harmful responses while preserving utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFE INFER, a two-phase decoding-time safety alignment strategy that combines safety amplification (adjusting hidden states with safe demonstrations) and safety-guided decoding (influencing token selection) to reduce harmful responses while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: SAFE INFER is an effective decoding-time safety alignment strategy that significantly reduces harmful responses across various models, datasets, and prompting techniques while maintaining the model's general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE INFER achieves the lowest attack success rates (ASR) across multiple safety datasets (e.g., 1.09% on HarmEval for Llama-2) compared to baselines like SafeDecoding and Self-CD.
The method is effective against various jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, DeepInception, GPTFuzzer), reducing ASR to near zero in some cases.
SAFE INFER preserves the utility of base models on benchmarks like MMLU and TruthfulQA, with minimal performance drop.
The method also works on edited models (using ROME), significantly reducing the increased harmfulness introduced by model editing.
SAFE INFER shows effectiveness across different prompting techniques: simple, instruction-centric, and instruction-centric chain-of-thought prompts.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models often exhibit fragile and imbalanced safety mechanisms, increasing the likelihood of generating unsafe content. In addition, incorporating new knowledge through editing techniques to language models can further compromise safety. To address these issues, we propose SafeInfer, a context-adaptive, decoding-time safety alignment strategy for generating safe responses to user queries. SafeInfer comprises two phases: the safety amplification phase, which employs safe demonstration examples to adjust the model's hidden states and increase the likelihood of safer outputs, and the safety-guided decoding phase, which influences token selection based on safety-optimized distributions, ensuring the generated content complies with ethical guidelines. Further, we present HarmEval, a novel benchmark for extensive safety evaluations, designed to address potential misuse scenarios in accordance with the policies of leading AI tech giants.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
papers.research_question: What features in prompts lead to successful jailbreaks in LLMs, and are they linear or non-linear?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak features in LLMs are non-linear and model-specific, and non-linear probes can guide effective latent-space interventions to increase or decrease jailbreak success.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak mechanisms are heterogeneous and non-linear, and the proposed methodology provides insights into the features driving jailbreak outcomes.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on prompt representations can predict jailbreak success with high accuracy.
Non-linear probes generalize better across layers than linear probes.
Jailbreak features are not universal; probes do not generalize well to unseen attack types.
Non-linear probe-guided interventions can effectively increase or decrease jailbreak success.
Features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaks have been a central focus of research regarding the safety and reliability of large language models (LLMs), yet the mechanisms underlying these attacks remain poorly understood. While previous studies have predominantly relied on linear methods to detect jailbreak attempts and model refusals, we take a different approach by examining both linear and non-linear features in prompts that lead to successful jailbreaks. First, we introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,800 jailbreak attempts spanning 35 diverse attack methods. Leveraging this dataset, we train linear and non-linear probes on hidden states of open-weight LLMs to predict jailbreak success. Probes achieve strong in-distribution accuracy but transfer is attack-family-specific, revealing that different jailbreaks are supported by distinct internal mechanisms rather than a single universal direction. To establish causal relevance, we construct probe-guided latent interventions that systematically shift compliance in the predicted direction. Interventions derived from non-linear probes produce larger and more reliable effects than those from linear probes, indicating that features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations. Overall, the results surface heterogeneous, non-linear structure in jailbreak mechanisms and provide a prompt-side methodology for recovering and testing the features that drive jailbreak outcomes.

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks. Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
papers.research_question: How vulnerable are LLMs to model tampering attacks (modifications to latent activations or weights), and can these attacks inform evaluators about LLM vulnerabilities to novel input-space attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces model tampering attacks as a complementary evaluation method for LLMs, showing that they can predict input-space vulnerabilities and that state-of-the-art unlearning methods are brittle to fine-tuning attacks.
papers.conclusion: Model tampering attacks enable substantially more rigorous evaluations of LLM capabilities and risks than input-space attacks alone, highlighting the difficulty of suppressing harmful capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Model tampering attacks are efficient and effective at eliciting harmful capabilities from LLMs.
Model robustness to a variety of capability elicitation attacks lies on a low-dimensional subspace.
The success rate of model tampering attacks correlates with and can conservatively estimate the success of held-out input-space attacks.
State-of-the-art unlearning methods can be reversed within a few steps of fine-tuning (sometimes as few as one step).
Representation rerouting (RR) achieved the highest unlearning score, but no unlearning method was robust to all attacks.
papers.limitation: Model tampering attack success on one task (WMDP-Bio) was not strongly predictive of model performance on a different task (UK AISI bio evaluation), suggesting a limitation in generalizing across task distributions.
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) risks and capabilities are increasingly being incorporated into AI risk management and governance frameworks. Currently, most risk evaluations are conducted by designing inputs that elicit harmful behaviors from the system. However, this approach suffers from two limitations. First, input-output evaluations cannot fully evaluate realistic risks from open-weight models. Second, the behaviors identified during any particular input-output evaluation can only lower-bound the model's worst-possible-case input-output behavior. As a complementary method for eliciting harmful behaviors, we propose evaluating LLMs with model tampering attacks which allow for modifications to latent activations or weights. We pit state-of-the-art techniques for removing harmful LLM capabilities against a suite of 5 input-space and 6 model tampering attacks. In addition to benchmarking these methods against each other, we show that (1) model resilience to capability elicitation attacks lies on a low-dimensional robustness subspace; (2) the success rate of model tampering attacks can empirically predict and offer conservative estimates for the success of held-out input-space attacks; and (3) state-of-the-art unlearning methods can easily be undone within 16 steps of fine-tuning. Together, these results highlight the difficulty of suppressing harmful LLM capabilities and show that model tampering attacks enable substantially more rigorous evaluations than input-space attacks alone.

papers.title: ReasoningGuard: Safeguarding Large Reasoning Models with Inference-time Safety Aha Moments
papers.research_question: How to safeguard Large Reasoning Models from jailbreak attacks during inference without requiring costly fine-tuning or expert knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ReasoningGuard, an inference-time safeguard that uses attention-based safety injection and scaling sampling to protect Large Reasoning Models from jailbreak attacks without fine-tuning, balancing safety and utility.
papers.conclusion: ReasoningGuard provides an effective and efficient inference-time safeguard for LRMs, balancing safety and utility without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
ReasoningGuard significantly reduces harmful outputs on AdvBench and SorryBench under various jailbreak attacks.
It outperforms seven existing defense methods in safety performance.
The method preserves model utility on safe queries, as shown on MMLU, GPQA, and MATH-500 benchmarks.
It mitigates exaggerated safety issues compared to other defenses, as evaluated on XSTest.
The approach adds minimal inference cost, with an average token generation time ratio of around 1.09.
papers.limitation: In rare cases, ReasoningGuard may have false positives in safety detection, leading to unsafe classifications for non-toxic content.
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in reasoning-intensive tasks, but they remain vulnerable to harmful content generation, particularly in the mid-to-late steps of their reasoning processes. Existing defense mechanisms, however, rely on costly fine-tuning and additional expert knowledge, which restricts their scalability. In this work, we propose ReasoningGuard, an inference-time safeguard for LRMs, which injects timely safety aha moments to steer harmless while helpful reasoning processes. Leveraging the model's internal attention behavior, our approach accurately identifies critical points in the reasoning path, and triggers spontaneous, safety-oriented reflection. To safeguard both the subsequent reasoning steps and the final answers, we further implement a scaling sampling strategy during the decoding phase, selecting the optimal reasoning path. Inducing minimal extra inference cost, ReasoningGuard effectively mitigates three types of jailbreak attacks, including the latest ones targeting the reasoning process of LRMs. Our approach outperforms seven existing safeguards, achieving state-of-the-art safety defenses while effectively avoiding the common exaggerated safety issues.

papers.title: Attributional Safety Failures in Large Language Models under Code-Mixed Perturbations
papers.research_question: Why do safety guardrails in large language models fail under code-mixed perturbations, and how can this be explained and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers attributional collapse as a cause of safety failures in LLMs under code-mixed inputs, introduces the Saliency Drift Attribution (SDA) framework to explain it, and proposes a lightweight translation-based restoration strategy.
papers.conclusion: Code-mixing poses a serious and overlooked safety risk for LLMs, driven by attributional collapse, but interpretability methods like SDA can guide practical mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attack Success Rates (ASR) spike from ~9% in monolingual English to ~69% under code-mixed inputs, with rates exceeding 90% in languages like Arabic and Hindi.
The Saliency Drift Attribution (SDA) framework shows safety-critical tokens lose attributional salience under code-mixing, blinding the model to harmful intent.
A translation-based restoration strategy recovers roughly 80% of the safety lost to code-mixing.
Safety failures persist on real-world social media data (TRAC-1), confirming the vulnerability is not an artifact of synthetic data.
The degree of safety degradation increases monotonically with the intensity of code-mixing (e.g., higher embedded language ratio).
papers.abstract: While LLMs appear robustly safety-aligned in English, we uncover a catastrophic, overlooked weakness: attributional collapse under code-mixed perturbations. Our systematic evaluation of open models shows that the linguistic camouflage of code-mixing -- ``blending languages within a single conversation'' -- can cause safety guardrails to fail dramatically. Attack success rates (ASR) spike from a benign 9\% in monolingual English to 69\% under code-mixed inputs, with rates exceeding 90\% in non-Western contexts such as Arabic and Hindi. These effects hold not only on controlled synthetic datasets but also on real-world social media traces, revealing a serious risk for billions of users. To explain why this happens, we introduce saliency drift attribution (SDA), an interpretability framework that shows how, under code-mixing, the model's internal attention drifts away from safety-critical tokens (e.g., ``violence'' or ``corruption''), effectively blinding it to harmful intent. Finally, we propose a lightweight translation-based restoration strategy that recovers roughly 80\% of the safety lost to code-mixing, offering a practical path toward more equitable and robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Advancing LLM Safe Alignment with Safety Representation Ranking
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM safety by leveraging internal representations to rank candidate responses without altering the model's decoding logic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that uses LLM internal representations to rank candidate responses by safety, without altering the model's decoding logic, improving robustness to adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: SRR serves as a practical and effective safeguard module for LLM alignment, offering a new paradigm for enhancing the safety and reliability of LLMs in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts across multiple benchmarks.
SRR generalizes well across different safety evaluation datasets.
SRR can be adapted to other alignment perspectives like privacy and fairness.
SRR maintains natural performance on benign tasks (e.g., mathematical reasoning).
SRR outperforms baseline reward models in safety ranking accuracy despite being much smaller.
papers.limitation:
SRR might need task-specific fine-tuning for optimal performance in certain situations.
SRR's adaptability to special-domain safety scenarios requires further testing.
