NeuroBreak enables progressive exploration from macroscopic behavior to neuron-level mechanisms in jailbreak attacks.
It identifies safety neurons and categorizes them into functional archetypes based on toxicity vectors and activation patterns.
The system reveals that layers 15-28 encode discriminative harmful features with high probe accuracy.
Targeted fine-tuning of safety neurons using NeuroBreak improves model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
NeuroBreak provides visual evidence for neuron cooperation patterns and vulnerabilities in LLM safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on linear probing may miss nonlinear semantic shifts influencing adversarial behaviors.
Lack of dynamic adversarial interactions or real-time adaptation to evolving threats.
future_direction: Explore nonlinear probing techniques for more complex decision boundaries.
Incorporate dynamic adversarial training or online learning for real-time adaptation.
papers.abstract: In deployment and application, large language models (LLMs) typically undergo safety alignment to prevent illegal and unethical outputs. However, the continuous advancement of jailbreak attack techniques, designed to bypass safety mechanisms with adversarial prompts, has placed increasing pressure on the security defenses of LLMs. Strengthening resistance to jailbreak attacks requires an in-depth understanding of the security mechanisms and vulnerabilities of LLMs. However, the vast number of parameters and complex structure of LLMs make analyzing security weaknesses from an internal perspective a challenging task. This paper presents NeuroBreak, a top-down jailbreak analysis system designed to analyze neuron-level safety mechanisms and mitigate vulnerabilities. We carefully design system requirements through collaboration with three experts in the field of AI security. The system provides a comprehensive analysis of various jailbreak attack methods. By incorporating layer-wise representation probing analysis, NeuroBreak offers a novel perspective on the model's decision-making process throughout its generation steps. Furthermore, the system supports the analysis of critical neurons from both semantic and functional perspectives, facilitating a deeper exploration of security mechanisms. We conduct quantitative evaluations and case studies to verify the effectiveness of our system, offering mechanistic insights for developing next-generation defense strategies against evolving jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: ConceptGuard: Neuro-Symbolic Safety Guardrails via Sparse Interpretable Jailbreak Concepts
papers.research_question: Can SAEs disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts representing jailbreak-related themes? Can these concepts facilitate interpretable, concept-guided guardrails that generalize across diverse jailbreak styles while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ConceptGuard, a framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders to extract interpretable jailbreak concepts from LLM activations and builds a linear guardrail that generalizes to stealthy jailbreaks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ConceptGuard demonstrates that interpretable jailbreak concepts can be extracted from LLM activations using SAEs and used to build a linear guardrail that generalizes across jailbreak styles without fine-tuning, offering a robust and transparent safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts corresponding to jailbreak themes.
The concept-guided guardrail (trained only on base attacks) generalizes to stealthy jailbreak styles (e.g., hypothetical, BoN) without exposure to them during training.
The pruned guardrail (using only rich features) reduces the feature space by 57% while maintaining competitive performance.
The guardrail outperforms baseline safety-tuned models (like Llama-Guard) in generalization.
The activation-based guardrails are robust to input perturbations that confuse the model, as shown by UMAP visualizations.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a single hook point (attention layer of the 8th transformer block).
The pruning heuristic might be overly aggressive and classify safety-critical features as junk.
The method assumes the model has undergone safety fine-tuning; effectiveness on unaligned models is unknown.
The linear classifier may not capture complex, non-linear interactions between jailbreak concepts.
future_direction: Using sparse-crosscoders to extract interacting harmful concepts across multiple layers.
Exploring more sophisticated methods to identify safety-critical features without relying strictly on token-level interpretability metrics.
Testing the method on unaligned foundational models and exploring more expressive classifiers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have found success in a variety of applications. However, their safety remains a concern due to the existence of various jailbreaking methods. Despite significant efforts, alignment and safety fine-tuning only provide a certain degree of robustness against jailbreak attacks that covertly mislead LLMs towards the generation of harmful content. This leaves them prone to a range of vulnerabilities, including targeted misuse and accidental user profiling. This work introduces \textbf{ConceptGuard}, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify interpretable concepts within LLM internals associated with different jailbreak themes. By extracting semantically meaningful internal representations, ConceptGuard enables building robust safety guardrails -- offering fully explainable and generalizable defenses without sacrificing model capabilities or requiring further fine-tuning. Leveraging advances in the mechanistic interpretability of LLMs, our approach provides evidence for a shared activation geometry for jailbreak attacks in the representation space, a potential foundation for designing more interpretable and generalizable safeguards against attackers.

papers.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the inherent immunity of conventionally aligned LLMs against existing jailbreak attacks without significantly sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DEEPALIGN, a fine-tuning method that uses contrastive hidden-state steering to enhance LLM safety by amplifying the separation between harmful and benign hidden states during generation, reducing jailbreak success while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: DEEPALIGN provides a unified, architecture-agnostic defense that significantly improves the safety-utility Pareto frontier by enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention during generation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates as generation progresses, reflected in diminishing separability of hidden states.
DEEPALIGN reduces attack success rates of diverse jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal levels across multiple LLMs.
DEEPALIGN preserves model utility and reduces over-refusal compared to baseline defenses.
The method's automated data generation diversifies safe response patterns, increasing resilience against attacks targeting limited refusal patterns.
DEEPALIGN maintains robustness against an adaptive attack derived from DrAttack.
papers.limitation: The adaptive attack presents a challenge by providing the model with a malicious yet seemingly benign response prefix, testing robustness against adversarial out-of-distribution prefixes.
papers.abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit adversarial prompts to circumvent safety measures. Current safety fine-tuning approaches face two critical limitations. First, they often fail to strike a balance between security and utility, where stronger safety measures tend to over-reject harmless user requests. Second, they frequently miss malicious intent concealed within seemingly benign tasks, leaving models exposed to exploitation. Our work identifies a fundamental cause of these issues: during response generation, an LLM's capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates. Experimental evidence confirms this, revealing that the separability between hidden states for safe and harmful responses diminishes as generation progresses. This weakening discrimination forces models to make compliance judgments earlier in the generation process, restricting their ability to recognize developing harmful intent and contributing to both aforementioned failures. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce DEEPALIGN - an inherent defense framework that enhances the safety of LLMs. By applying contrastive hidden-state steering at the midpoint of response generation, DEEPALIGN amplifies the separation between harmful and benign hidden states, enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention throughout the generation process. Across diverse LLMs spanning varying architectures and scales, it reduced attack success rates of nine distinct jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal. Crucially, it preserved model capability while reducing over-refusal. Models equipped with DEEPALIGN exhibited up to 3.5% lower error rates in rejecting challenging benign queries and maintained standard task performance with less than 1% decline. This marks a substantial advance in the safety-utility Pareto frontier.

papers.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models by unlearning harmful outputs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeLLM, a token-level unlearning framework that integrates dynamic detection, FFN activation tracing, and constrained optimization to suppress harmful outputs in LLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving general performance.
papers.conclusion: SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behavior, significantly reducing jailbreak attack success rates without degrading general performance, offering a scalable and proactive defense for LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
SafeLLM significantly reduces Attack Success Rates (ASR) across jailbreak benchmarks compared to baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
It maintains general performance on benign datasets such as OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA after unlearning.
SafeLLM enables irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviors by targeting FFN substructures responsible for harmful token generation.
The framework demonstrates robustness to unseen adversarial prompts through feature-driven generalization.
Ablation studies show that dynamic fusion weights and adaptive trust-region bounds optimize the safety-utility trade-off.
future_direction: Advance unlearning techniques to tackle broader challenges related to fairness, transparency, and adversarial threats in multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose a serious threat to the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) by crafting adversarial prompts that bypass alignment mechanisms, causing the models to produce harmful, restricted, or biased content. In this paper, we propose SafeLLM, a novel unlearning-based defense framework that unlearn the harmful knowledge from LLMs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities. SafeLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic unsafe output detection using a hybrid approach that integrates external classifiers with model-internal evaluations; (2) token-level harmful content tracing through feedforward network (FFN) activations to localize harmful knowledge; and (3) constrained optimization to suppress unsafe behavior without degrading overall model quality. SafeLLM achieves targeted and irreversible forgetting by identifying and neutralizing FFN substructures responsible for harmful generation pathways. Extensive experiments on prominent LLMs (Vicuna, LLaMA, and GPT-J) across multiple jailbreak benchmarks show that SafeLLM substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining high general-purpose performance. Compared to standard defense methods such as supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, SafeLLM offers stronger safety guarantees, more precise control over harmful behavior, and greater robustness to unseen attacks. Moreover, SafeLLM maintains the general performance after the harmful knowledge unlearned. These results highlight unlearning as a promising direction for scalable and effective LLM safety.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: A Representation Engineering Perspective on the Effectiveness of Multi-Turn Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: How do language models represent multi-turn jailbreak (Crescendo) inputs compared to single-turn inputs? How does the number of conversation turns affect these representations, and how do the model's own responses influence them?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-turn jailbreaks like Crescendo cause safety-aligned language models to represent harmful outputs as benign, especially as the number of turns increases, explaining why single-turn defenses like circuit breakers fail to generalize.
papers.conclusion: There is a generalization gap between single-turn defenses and multi-turn jailbreaks, motivating the development of defenses that target harmful multi-turn representations.
papers.key_findings:
Crescendo attacks cause models to represent the final harmful response tokens as more benign than harmful.
Increasing the number of turns in a Crescendo conversation decreases the model's representation of the output as harmful.
User prompts in the attack play a primary role in shaping representations towards benign regions; the model's own prior responses have a smaller effect.
Single-turn jailbreak defenses (circuit breakers) show a generalization gap and are ineffective against multi-turn attacks.
Crescendo works by keeping the model in a benign region of representation space across turns, tricking it into generating harmful content.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to know how much the MLP probe results capture the model's internal notion of 'harmfulness' versus other differences between training and Crescendo representations.
The analysis focuses exclusively on the Crescendo jailbreak method.
future_direction: Explore whether the observations hold for other multi-turn jailbreaks like GOAT and Tempest.
Expand the analysis to more models, including reasoning models and other leading jailbreak defenses.
Develop better defenses that target both single-turn and multi-turn model representations.
papers.abstract: Recent research has demonstrated that state-of-the-art LLMs and defenses remain susceptible to multi-turn jailbreak attacks. These attacks require only closed-box model access and are often easy to perform manually, posing a significant threat to the safe and secure deployment of LLM-based systems. We study the effectiveness of the Crescendo multi-turn jailbreak at the level of intermediate model representations and find that safety-aligned LMs often represent Crescendo responses as more benign than harmful, especially as the number of conversation turns increases. Our analysis indicates that at each turn, Crescendo prompts tend to keep model outputs in a "benign" region of representation space, effectively tricking the model into fulfilling harmful requests. Further, our results help explain why single-turn jailbreak defenses like circuit breakers are generally ineffective against multi-turn attacks, motivating the development of mitigations that address this generalization gap.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety against adversarial reasoning exploits by training models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and providing interpretable, context-aware safety.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning (RATIONAL) enables LLMs to internalize safety-aware reasoning, improving robustness against adversarial attacks and providing interpretable, context-aware responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL reduces attack success rates on adversarial benchmarks (SorryBench, HarmBench) to very low levels.
RATIONAL generalizes to unseen attack types (gradient-based and persona-based) without direct training.
RATIONAL improves truthfulness and reduces toxicity (as shown on TruthfulQA and ToxiGen).
RATIONAL balances safety and helpfulness, reducing over-refusals on benign queries.
The ablation study shows that both reasoning and adversarial data are important: writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning, but persuasion attacks require adversarial examples.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks but may require complementary strategies to defend against emerging attack techniques, such as adaptive multi-turn exploits.
future_direction: Improving robustness and helpfulness simultaneously via reasoning-based alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs.While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making.To address this, we propose ReAsoning-enhanced Fine-TunIng fOr iNterpretAble LLM Safety (RATIONAL), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response.Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in selfgenerated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making.Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety.RATIONAL employs reasoningenhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: DELMAN: Dynamic Defense Against Large Language Model Jailbreaking with Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models in a dynamic, precise, and minimal way during the deployment phase?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DELMAN, a dynamic defense mechanism that directly edits a minimal set of model parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors from jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility on normal tasks.
papers.conclusion: DELMAN demonstrates how token-level direct model editing can effectively enhance LLM safety against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance, offering a practical solution for post-deployment protection.
papers.key_findings:
DELMAN significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across multiple jailbreak attack types and datasets, often to 0%.
DELMAN preserves or even improves model utility on general-purpose and downstream tasks compared to baseline defenses.
DELMAN's edits are transferable across different harmful behaviors and datasets due to overlapping representations of harmful tokens.
DELMAN supports consecutive edits without interfering with previous modifications, enabling dynamic defense updates.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to general-purpose LLMs, leaving applicability to domain-specialized models and larger-scale models unexplored.
DELMAN relies on GPT-4 for harmful token extraction and context generation, introducing dependency on external models and potential cost barriers.
The stability of consecutive edits, though preliminarily validated, needs deeper analysis to assess potential performance drift over extended deployment.
future_direction: Investigate more efficient methods for harmful token identification, e.g., using a minimal set of tokens to cover the majority of harmful scenarios.
Explore the application of DELMAN to domain-specific LLMs and VLMs to validate its generalizability across different domains and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely applied in decision making, but their deployment is threatened by jailbreak attacks, where adversarial users manipulate model behavior to bypass safety measures. Existing defense mechanisms, such as safety fine-tuning and model editing, either require extensive parameter modifications or lack precision, leading to performance degradation on general tasks, which is unsuitable to post-deployment safety alignment. To address these challenges, we propose DELMAN (Dynamic Editing for LLMs JAilbreak DefeNse), a novel approach leveraging direct model editing for precise, dynamic protection against jailbreak attacks. DELMAN directly updates a minimal set of relevant parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors while preserving the model's utility. To avoid triggering a safe response in benign context, we incorporate KL-divergence regularization to ensure the updated model remains consistent with the original model when processing benign queries. Experimental results demonstrate that DELMAN outperforms baseline methods in mitigating jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility, and adapts seamlessly to new attack instances, providing a practical and efficient solution for post-deployment model protection.

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: AttnGCG: Enhancing Jailbreaking Attacks on LLMs with Attention Manipulation
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaking attacks on LLMs be enhanced by manipulating the models' attention scores?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttnGCG, an enhanced jailbreaking attack that manipulates LLMs' attention scores to increase focus on adversarial suffixes, leading to higher attack success rates and improved transferability.
papers.conclusion: Attention manipulation is an effective strategy for enhancing jailbreaking attacks on LLMs, and visualizing attention scores offers clear insights into the attack mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
A positive correlation exists between the attention score on the adversarial suffix and the attack success rate (ASR).
AttnGCG consistently outperforms the GCG baseline across various LLMs, achieving an average ASR increase of ~6.3% (GPT-4 judge).
AttnGCG reduces the gap between keyword-based and GPT-4 judge ASR, indicating a reduction in false jailbreaks.
AttnGCG demonstrates strong transferability, improving ASR on unseen harmful goals by an average of 11.4% and on black-box LLMs like GPT-4 by 2.8%.
Attention score visualization provides interpretable insights into how jailbreaking exploits attention distributions.
papers.limitation: The transfer attack performance of AttnGCG is unsatisfactory on the latest models (Gemini-1.5-Pro-latest, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-4o), necessitating further research.
future_direction: Further research to improve transfer attack performance on the latest LLM models.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the vulnerabilities of transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to jailbreaking attacks, focusing specifically on the optimization-based Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) strategy. We first observe a positive correlation between the effectiveness of attacks and the internal behaviors of the models. For instance, attacks tend to be less effective when models pay more attention to system prompts designed to ensure LLM safety alignment. Building on this discovery, we introduce an enhanced method that manipulates models' attention scores to facilitate LLM jailbreaking, which we term AttnGCG. Empirically, AttnGCG shows consistent improvements in attack efficacy across diverse LLMs, achieving an average increase of ~7% in the Llama-2 series and ~10% in the Gemma series. Our strategy also demonstrates robust attack transferability against both unseen harmful goals and black-box LLMs like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Moreover, we note our attention-score visualization is more interpretable, allowing us to gain better insights into how our targeted attention manipulation facilitates more effective jailbreaking. We release the code at https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/AttnGCG-attack.

papers.title: One Trigger Token Is Enough: A Defense Strategy for Balancing Safety and Usability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we defend LLMs against jailbreak attacks by identifying and decoding safety trigger tokens that activate the model's safety patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes D-STT, a defense algorithm that identifies and decodes safety trigger tokens to activate a model's learned safety patterns, effectively defending against jailbreak attacks while preserving usability with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: D-STT provides a simple, effective, and lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by explicitly decoding safety trigger tokens, balancing safety and usability with negligible latency.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow safety alignment in LLMs manifests through learned 'safety trigger tokens' that activate safety patterns when paired with harmful input.
Safety trigger tokens are highly similar across different harmful inputs, enabling cross-sample learning and generalization.
D-STT significantly reduces output harmfulness against diverse jailbreak attacks while maintaining high response quality on benign prompts.
Constraining the safety trigger to a single token effectively balances safety and usability with minimal intervention.
D-STT is lightweight, incurring only 2% response time overhead, and outperforms ten baseline defense methods.
papers.limitation:
Relies on collecting refusal samples and the explicit output vocabulary distribution; future work may explore identifying triggers directly from the model's feature space.
Requires intervention in the decoding process, making it inapplicable for end-users of closed-source, black-box commercial models where inference parameters are inaccessible.
future_direction: Explore how to identify the 'trigger' nature of safety tokens directly from the model's feature space (e.g., hidden states or attention patterns).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively used across diverse domains, including virtual assistants, automated code generation, and scientific research. However, they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, which manipulate the models into generating harmful responses despite safety alignment. Recent studies have shown that current safety-aligned LLMs undergo shallow safety alignment. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation into the underlying mechanism of this phenomenon and reveal that it manifests through learned ''safety trigger tokens'' that activate the model's safety patterns when paired with the specific input. Through both analysis and empirical verification, we further demonstrate the high similarity of the safety trigger tokens across different harmful inputs. Accordingly, we propose D-STT, a simple yet effective defense algorithm that identifies and explicitly decodes safety trigger tokens of the given safety-aligned LLM to activate the model's learned safety patterns. In this process, the safety trigger is constrained to a single token, which effectively preserves model usability by introducing minimum intervention in the decoding process. Extensive experiments across diverse jailbreak attacks and benign prompts demonstrate that D-STT significantly reduces output harmfulness while preserving model usability and incurring negligible response time overhead, outperforming ten baseline methods.

papers.title: From Theft to Bomb-Making: The Ripple Effect of Unlearning in Defending Against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: Can unlearning generalize to harmful knowledge that was not explicitly encountered during training? For instance, if a model is trained to forget how to steal goods, could it also implicitly forget how to construct a bomb?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and empirically validates the ripple effect in unlearning, showing that unlearning specific harmful knowledge can generalize to unseen harmful knowledge, making it an effective defense against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning exhibits a ripple effect, generalizing to unseen harmful knowledge, and is a promising defense against jailbreak attacks. Future work is needed to fully understand its limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning-based methods can generalize to out-of-distribution harmful knowledge, reducing attack success rate from over 70% to less than 10% with only 100 training samples.
The generalization ability stems from the intrinsic relatedness among harmful responses, as seen in clustered hidden representations.
Unlearning harmful responses is more effective than only learning safe responses (SFT) because harmful responses are similar across different jailbreak prompts.
Unlearning can sometimes lead to over-refusal, but this can be mitigated by incorporating adversarially benign queries during training.
There are challenging scenarios for unlearning, such as dispersed harmful knowledge (e.g., writing persuasive articles) and subtle/implicit risks.
papers.limitation:
Unlearning may struggle with dispersed harmful knowledge (e.g., writing persuasive articles) and subtle/implicit risks.
Experiments are limited to certain models (Llama-3.1 and Mistral-v0.3) and attack methods, leaving others for future work.
future_direction: Systematic investigation of the impact of unlearning on benign knowledge.
Testing on more models and jailbreak attack methods.
Exploring the reasons behind the clustering of harmful responses in the model's hidden representations.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. An important observation is that, while different types of jailbreak attacks can generate significantly different queries, they mostly result in similar responses that are rooted in the same harmful knowledge (e.g., detailed steps to make a bomb). Consequently, unlearning-based approaches have been proposed to mitigate jailbreak attacks by directly removing harmful knowledge from the model. In this paper, we identify a novel ripple effect of unlearning, wherein LLMs can implicitly unlearn harmful knowledge that was not explicitly introduced during the unlearning phase (e.g., a model unlearning the steps for theft may also implicitly unlearn the steps for making a bomb). Through over 100 experimental runs spanning multiple models, attack strategies, and defense methods, we empirically validate this phenomenon, which makes unlearning-based methods able to decrease the Attack Success Rate on unseen data from more than 70% to less than 10% with only 100 training samples. Further analysis reveals that the strong generalization ability of unlearning may stem from the intrinsic relatedness among harmful responses across harmful questions (e.g., response patterns, shared steps and actions in response, and similarity among their learned representations in the LLM). We also discuss the potential limitations of unlearning and the observed ripple effect. We hope our research could contribute to a deeper understanding of unlearning. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-coai/SafeUnlearning.

papers.title: Model-Editing-Based Jailbreak against Safety-aligned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a more stealthy jailbreak attack vector for LLMs that minimizes user involvement by directly modifying internal model structures to bypass safety alignment without input modifications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Targeted Model Editing (TME), a white-box jailbreak method that bypasses safety filters by identifying and removing safety-critical transformations (SCTs) from MLP weight matrices, enabling harmful responses without input modifications while preserving normal model functionality.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security via model editing-based jailbreaks and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations for unsafe samples are highly consistent (due to uniform refusal), while activations for safe samples are more variable.
The difference in average activation values between safe and unsafe samples is significantly larger than the variation within unsafe samples.
The overlap rate of activated neurons between safe and unsafe inputs is low (below 25%), indicating distinct processing pathways.
The D-LLM framework, which implements TME, achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% across four open-source LLMs.
The method maintains model performance on standard benchmarks (TruthfulQA, MMLU) after editing, showing preserved functionality.
future_direction: Further unveil the vulnerabilities of D-LLM and provide insights for LLM developers to bolster safety.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous fields by enabling advanced natural language interactions but remain susceptible to critical vulnerabilities, particularly jailbreak attacks. Current jailbreak techniques, while effective, often depend on input modifications, making them detectable and limiting their stealth and scalability. This paper presents Targeted Model Editing (TME), a novel white-box approach that bypasses safety filters by minimally altering internal model structures while preserving the model's intended functionalities. TME identifies and removes safety-critical transformations (SCTs) embedded in model matrices, enabling malicious queries to bypass restrictions without input modifications. By analyzing distinct activation patterns between safe and unsafe queries, TME isolates and approximates SCTs through an optimization process. Implemented in the D-LLM framework, our method achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% on four mainstream open-source LLMs, maintaining high performance. Unlike existing methods, D-LLM eliminates the need for specific triggers or harmful response collections, offering a stealthier and more effective jailbreak strategy. This work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.

papers.title: Shaping the Safety Boundaries: Understanding and Defending Against Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does jailbreaking operate in large language models, and how can we develop an effective defense mechanism based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that jailbreaks shift harmful activations beyond a safety boundary, especially in low and middle layers, and proposes a novel defense (ABD) that constrains activations within this boundary to prevent harmful outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive analysis of jailbreak mechanisms, showing they shift activations outside a safety boundary, and proposes ABD, an effective and efficient defense that leverages this understanding by constraining activations within the boundary.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts shift activations outside a defined safety boundary, with the most severe shifts occurring in the low and middle layers of the model.
The safety boundary expands in deeper layers, requiring larger activation shifts to bypass safety checks.
The proposed Activation Boundary Defense (ABD) effectively constrains jailbreak activations within the safety boundary, achieving high defense success rates (over 98% on average) with minimal impact (less than 2%) on the model's general capabilities.
Bayesian optimization for layer selection in ABD confirms that low and middle layers are the most critical for defense, aligning with the mechanistic findings.
papers.limitation:
ABD may underperform on under-aligned models because unclear safety boundaries complicate the search for effective penalty functions.
The analysis and defense focus on single-round jailbreak scenarios and do not extend to multi-turn dialogues or long-context attacks.
future_direction: Investigate the challenges of jailbreaks in multi-turn dialogue scenarios.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking in Large Language Models (LLMs) is a major security concern as it can deceive LLMs to generate harmful text. Yet, there is still insufficient understanding of how jailbreaking works, which makes it hard to develop effective defense strategies. We aim to shed more light into this issue: we conduct a detailed large-scale analysis of seven different jailbreak methods and find that these disagreements stem from insufficient observation samples. In particular, we introduce \textit{safety boundary}, and we find that jailbreaks shift harmful activations outside that safety boundary, where LLMs are less sensitive to harmful information. We also find that the low and the middle layers are critical in such shifts, while deeper layers have less impact. Leveraging on these insights, we propose a novel defense called \textbf{Activation Boundary Defense} (ABD), which adaptively constrains the activations within the safety boundary. We further use Bayesian optimization to selectively apply the defense method to the low and the middle layers. Our experiments on several benchmarks show that ABD achieves an average DSR of over 98\% against various forms of jailbreak attacks, with less than 2\% impact on the model's general capabilities.

papers.title: DeTAM: Defending LLMs Against Jailbreak Attacks via Targeted Attention Modification
papers.research_question: How to defend LLMs against jailbreak attacks without fine-tuning by modifying attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DETAM, a finetuning-free defense method that improves LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by identifying and modifying sensitive attention heads to reallocate attention towards user intent and away from attack tokens.
papers.conclusion: DETAM effectively defends against jailbreak attacks by targeted attention modification, demonstrating superior performance and generalization while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
DETAM outperforms existing defense methods in reducing Attack Success Rate across various jailbreak attacks.
DETAM shows strong generalization across different LLMs and attack types, including on in-the-wild jailbreak data.
DETAM maintains a better balance between safety and utility, with lower false refusal rates compared to other defenses.
The method identifies sensitive attention heads by analyzing attention distribution differences between successful and unsuccessful defenses.
Attention heads selected by DETAM can be transferred to other models within the same family without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Increasing the number of modified attention heads can degrade the model's generative capabilities, especially for models without alignments.
Evaluation is limited to existing jailbreak attack techniques; future attacks may require broader defense methods.
future_direction: Design defenses that minimize impact on benign samples by improving attention head localization.
Develop adaptive defense mechanisms that adjust based on model complexity and attack variation.
Expand the scope of defense methods to address a broader range of attacks as jailbreak techniques evolve.
papers.abstract: Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful outputs.With the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), jailbreak attacks have become an increasingly pressing safety concern.While safety-aligned LLMs can effectively defend against normal harmful queries, they remain vulnerable to such attacks.Existing defense methods primarily rely on finetuning or input modification, which often suffer from limited generalization and reduced utility.To address this, we introduce DETAM, a finetuning-free defense approach that improves the defensive capabilities against jailbreak attacks of LLMs via targeted attention modification.Specifically, we analyze the differences in attention scores between successful and unsuccessful defenses to identify the attention heads sensitive to jailbreak attacks.During inference, we reallocate attention to emphasize users' core intentions, minimizing interference from attack tokens.Our experimental results demonstrate that DETAM outperforms various baselines in jailbreak defense and exhibits robust generalization across different attacks and models, maintaining its effectiveness even on in-thewild jailbreak data.Furthermore, we compare DETAM with the baselines on over-defense datasets, further validating its superior balance between helpfulness and harmlessness.

papers.title: How Jailbreak Defenses Work and Ensemble? A Mechanistic Investigation
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak defenses work in terms of safety shift and harmfulness discrimination, and how can they be ensembled to balance safety and helpfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies two core mechanisms in jailbreak defenses (safety shift and harmfulness discrimination) and proposes inter-mechanism and intra-mechanism ensemble strategies to improve safety or balance it with helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed ensemble defense strategies, based on the identified safety shift and harmfulness discrimination mechanisms, effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Safety shift defenses increase refusal probabilities for both harmful and benign queries, improving safety but risking over-defense and reduced helpfulness.
Harmfulness discrimination defenses improve the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign queries, mitigating over-defense.
Inter-mechanism ensembles (combining methods with the same mechanism) amplify a single defense mechanism, while intra-mechanism ensembles (combining safety shift and harmfulness discrimination methods) achieve a better trade-off.
Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, with individual methods showing limited success rates, but ensemble strategies can improve performance.
Fine-tuning with safety-focused datasets (e.g., SPA-VL) can improve safety, but dataset choice (e.g., VLGuard) can lead to over-defense, which can be mitigated by adding general instruction data.
papers.limitation: Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, and all individual defense methods still exhibit limited defense success rates.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks, where harmful prompts bypass generative models' built-in safety, raise serious concerns about model vulnerability. While many defense methods have been proposed, the trade-offs between safety and helpfulness, and their application to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), are not well understood. This paper systematically examines jailbreak defenses by reframing the standard generation task as a binary classification problem to assess model refusal tendencies for both harmful and benign queries. We identify two key defense mechanisms: safety shift, which increases refusal rates across all queries, and harmfulness discrimination, which improves the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign inputs. Using these mechanisms, we develop two ensemble defense strategies-inter-mechanism ensembles and intra-mechanism ensembles-to balance safety and helpfulness. Experiments on the MM-SafetyBench and MOSSBench datasets with LLaVA-1.5 models show that these strategies effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

papers.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
papers.research_question: How vulnerable is the refusal property of language models, learned through safety alignment training, to bit-wise errors induced by practical fault-injection attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISONBREAK, an efficient bit-selection algorithm to jailbreak large language models by flipping a small number of bits in model parameters, demonstrating vulnerability to bit-flip attacks.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight a pressing, practical threat to the language model ecosystem and underscore the need for research to protect these models from bit-flip attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks billion-parameter LLMs with only 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40× fewer bit flips than prior attacks.
Certain model components, such as value projection layers, are disproportionately vulnerable to bit-flips.
The attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods, not relying on prompt modifications.
Models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak.
Effective end-to-end exploitation via Rowhammer on GDDR6 GPUs, achieving high attack success rates.
future_direction: Further exploration of jailbreaking quantized models
papers.abstract: We study a new vulnerability in commercial-scale safety-aligned large language models (LLMs): their refusal to generate harmful responses can be broken by flipping only a few bits in model parameters. Our attack jailbreaks billion-parameter language models with just 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40$\times$ fewer bit flips than prior attacks on much smaller computer vision models. Unlike prompt-based jailbreaks, our method directly uncensors models in memory at runtime, enabling harmful outputs without requiring input-level modifications. Our key innovation is an efficient bit-selection algorithm that identifies critical bits for language model jailbreaks up to 20$\times$ faster than prior methods. We evaluate our attack on 10 open-source LLMs, achieving high attack success rates (ASRs) of 80-98% with minimal impact on model utility. We further demonstrate an end-to-end exploit via Rowhammer-based fault injection, reliably jailbreaking 5 models (69-91% ASR) on a GDDR6 GPU. Our analyses reveal that: (1) models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak; (2) certain model components, e.g., value projection layers, are substantially more vulnerable; and (3) the attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods. We evaluate potential countermeasures and find that our attack remains effective against defenses at various stages of the LLM pipeline.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
Progressive intervention analysis shows that model behavior transitions from complete refusal to full harmful compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold, with further intervention leading to degraded language capabilities.
papers.limitation:
No defense strategies have been developed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities.
The approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Evaluation is limited to a set of open-source models and English-language instructions; generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
future_direction: Developing robust safeguards based on the insights from GOSV.
Extending the approach to black-box scenarios.
Investigating generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Rebuilding LLMs Safety Mechanism via Probabilistically Ablating Refusal Direction
papers.research_question: How can we make large language models more robust against jailbreak attacks by rebuilding their safety mechanisms via probabilistically ablating the refusal direction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepRefusal, a safety alignment framework that forces LLMs to dynamically rebuild refusal mechanisms from jailbreak states by probabilistically ablating the refusal direction across layers and token depths during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: DeepRefusal bridges the gap between surface-level alignment and robust internal defense by forcing models to rebuild safety mechanisms from jailbreak states, offering a principled way to enhance LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
DeepRefusal reduces attack success rates by approximately 95% across various jailbreak attacks.
It effectively defends against prefilling attacks and refusal direction attacks, including transfer attacks.
The method maintains model capabilities (e.g., on MMLU, GSM8k) with minimal performance degradation.
