Evaluation is limited to a fixed set of models under single-turn prompting, and attention-entropy analysis provides only correlational evidence.
The work is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, with no concrete mitigation mechanisms proposed.
future_direction: Extend MIR-SafetyBench to more realistic user interactions, additional modalities and relation types, and richer measurements of internal states and real-world safety impact.
Bridge the gap from characterization to practical mitigation with detection mechanisms, safety monitors, or training-time regularizers.
papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) acquire stronger reasoning capabilities to handle complex, multi-image instructions, this advancement may pose new safety risks. We study this problem by introducing MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark focused on multi-image reasoning safety, which consists of 2,676 instances across a taxonomy of 9 multi-image relations. Our extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs reveal a troubling trend: models with more advanced multi-image reasoning can be more vulnerable on MIR-SafetyBench. Beyond attack success rates, we find that many responses labeled as safe are superficial, often driven by misunderstanding or evasive, non-committal replies. We further observe that unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average. This internal signature suggests a possible risk that models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/MIR-SafetyBench.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Jailbreaking Large Language Models via Attention Shifting
papers.research_question: What are the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs, and how can attention shifting be leveraged to improve such attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ASJA, a multi-turn jailbreak method that shifts LLM attention away from harmful keywords by fabricating dialogue history using a genetic algorithm, achieving higher attack success rates and stealthiness.
papers.conclusion: ASJA effectively breaks the LLM's safety alignment by shifting attention to historical queries and responses via fabricated dialogue, outperforming baselines in effectiveness, stealthiness, and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Successful multi-turn jailbreaks shift LLM attention away from harmful keywords to dialogue history, especially previous responses.
ASJA achieves higher attack success rates (44.91% improvement in harmfulness and 34.02% in relevance) compared to baselines.
ASJA maintains stealthiness (low perplexity) and has good transferability to other models.
The attention on harmful keywords in the last query is significantly lower in successful jailbreaks.
Optimizing both queries and responses in dialogue history is more effective than optimizing queries alone.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant performance in various natural language processing tasks but also pose safety and ethical threats, thus requiring red teaming and alignment processes to bolster their safety. To effectively exploit these aligned LLMs, recent studies have introduced jailbreak attacks based on multi-turn dialogues. These attacks aim to prompt LLMs to generate harmful or biased content by guiding them through contextual content. However, the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreaks remain unclear. Existing attacks often focus on optimizing queries and escalating toxicity to construct dialogues, lacking a thorough analysis of the inherent vulnerabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis of the differences between single-turn and multi-turn jailbreaks and find that successful multi-turn jailbreaks can effectively disperse the attention of LLMs on keywords associated with harmful behaviors, especially in historical responses. Based on this, we propose ASJA, a new multi-turn jailbreak approach by shifting the attention of LLMs, specifically by iteratively fabricating the dialogue history through a genetic algorithm to induce LLMs to generate harmful content. Extensive experiments on three LLMs and two datasets show that our approach surpasses existing approaches in jailbreak effectiveness, the stealth of jailbreak prompts, and attack efficiency. Our work emphasizes the importance of enhancing the robustness of LLMs' attention mechanism in multi-turn dialogue scenarios for a better defense strategy.

papers.title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs contain unsafe internal reasoning patterns even when the model's final output refuses a harmful request?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that CoT reasoning in LLMs often contains unsafe internal narratives even when the model refuses harmful requests, and introduces a framework to localize safety-critical layers and attention heads using Jacobian-based spectral metrics.
papers.conclusion: CoT is not inherently safe, and surface-level refusal does not guarantee safety in the internal reasoning process; the proposed framework provides a mechanistic understanding to mitigate latent reasoning risks.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 80% of reasoning chains harbor latent security risks even when models refuse harmful requests.
Safety-critical routing decisions are concentrated in a few contiguous mid-depth layers.
Jacobian-based metrics (stability, geometry, energy) can identify critical attention heads responsible for unsafe reasoning.
Perturbing critical attention heads leads to safety degradation, confirming their causal role in unsafe reasoning.
papers.abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures: stability, geometry, and energy to quantify how specific attention heads respond or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rise significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers. By precisely identifying the attention heads responsible for this divergence, our work challenges the assumption that refusal implies safety and provides a new understanding perspective for mitigating latent reasoning risks.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does activation steering, a technique for precise and interpretable model control, compromise LLM safety by systematically breaking alignment safeguards?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering, a technique promoted for precise and interpretable model control, systematically breaks LLM alignment safeguards, enabling harmful compliance even with random or semantically benign steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering poses systematic safety risks by breaking alignment safeguards, even with benign vectors, challenging the paradigm of safety through interpretability. Mitigation strategies and further research into the underlying mechanisms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1–13% across different model families.
Steering with benign SAE features demonstrates comparable or greater harmful potential, increasing compliance by 1–4% over random steering.
Steering is most effective when applied to the model's middle or early layers, indicating safety mechanisms are most vulnerable in intermediate processing stages.
Most SAE features exhibit jailbreaking capabilities, but they show poor cross-prompt generalization, making systematic safety monitoring challenging.
Averaging just 20 random vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack vector that significantly boosts harmful compliance on unseen requests, requiring only black-box steering access.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms behind alignment failures by analyzing activation patterns or refusal circuits in the model’s latent space.
Develop mitigation strategies like adversarial training to counter steering perturbations.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a promising technique for controlling LLM behavior by adding semantically meaningful vectors directly into a model's hidden states during inference. It is often framed as a precise, interpretable, and potentially safer alternative to fine-tuning. We demonstrate the opposite: steering systematically breaks model alignment safeguards, making it comply with harmful requests. Through extensive experiments on different model families, we show that even steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1-13%. Alarmingly, steering benign features from a sparse autoencoder (SAE), a common source of interpretable directions, demonstrates a comparable harmful potential. Finally, we show that combining 20 randomly sampled vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack, significantly increasing harmful compliance on unseen requests. These results challenge the paradigm of safety through interpretability, showing that precise control over model internals does not guarantee precise control over model behavior.

papers.title: ReGA: Representation-Guided Abstraction for Model-based Safeguarding of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we safeguard Large Language Models (LLMs) against harmful prompts and generations using a scalable, model-based analysis framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ReGA, a model-based safeguarding framework for LLMs that uses representation-guided abstraction to address scalability issues and effectively distinguish safe and harmful inputs.
papers.conclusion: ReGA is an efficient and scalable solution for LLM safety, integrating representation engineering with model abstraction to provide a new paradigm for safeguarding LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ReGA achieves high AUROC (0.975 at prompt level, 0.985 at conversation level) in distinguishing safe and harmful inputs.
ReGA generalizes to unseen datasets and shows robustness against various jailbreaking attacks.
ReGA outperforms other detection-based defense paradigms (MLP classifier, universal abstraction, LLM-Judge, perplexity filters) in effectiveness, interpretability, and scalability.
The framework is efficient and scalable, requiring only a few abstract states (8-64) compared to universal abstraction methods.
ReGA's performance is consistent across multiple LLMs, though weaker on models with lower reasoning capacity (e.g., koala).
papers.limitation:
Relies on a contrastive dataset, where bias or insufficient coverage may result in inaccurate safety representations.
May have limitations in generalizing to other LLMs, tasks, or safety perspectives due to differences in model architectures and data distributions.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant success in various tasks, yet concerns about their safety and security have emerged. In particular, they pose risks in generating harmful content and vulnerability to jailbreaking attacks. To analyze and monitor machine learning models, model-based analysis has demonstrated notable potential in stateful deep neural networks, yet suffers from scalability issues when extending to LLMs due to their vast feature spaces. In this paper, we propose ReGA, a model-based analysis framework with representation-guided abstraction, to safeguard LLMs against harmful prompts and generations. By leveraging safety-critical representations, which are low-dimensional directions emerging in hidden states that indicate safety-related concepts, ReGA effectively addresses the scalability issue when constructing the abstract model for safety modeling. Our comprehensive evaluation shows that ReGA performs sufficiently well in distinguishing between safe and harmful inputs, achieving an AUROC of 0.975 at the prompt level and 0.985 at the conversation level. Additionally, ReGA exhibits robustness to real-world attacks and generalization across different safety perspectives, outperforming existing safeguard paradigms in terms of interpretability and scalability. Overall, ReGA serves as an efficient and scalable solution to enhance LLM safety by integrating representation engineering with model-based abstraction, paving the way for new paradigms to utilize software insights for AI safety. Our code is available at https://github.com/weizeming/ReGA.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method. We find that LLaMA-2 is much safer on AdvBench prompts than on our dataset when evaluated with manual jailbreak attempts, and that pruning is effective against both automated attacks and manual jailbreaking on Advbench.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Jailbreak Attack Initializations as Extractors of Compliance Directions
papers.research_question: How do gradient-based jailbreak attack initializations work, and how can we design an initialization framework that effectively projects prompts along compliance directions to improve attack success rate and reduce computational overhead?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based jailbreak attacks and their initializations converge to a single compliance direction, and introduces the CRI framework to project unseen prompts along this direction, improving attack success rates and reducing computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that gradient-based jailbreak attacks converge to a single compliance direction and proposes CRI, an initialization framework that projects prompts along this direction, enhancing attack success rates and reducing computational overhead across various attacks, models, and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based jailbreak attacks and self-transfer initializations gradually converge to similar compliance directions.
The Loss at First Step (LFS) metric reliably indicates the number of steps required for a successful attack, enabling selection of effective initializations.
The CRI framework effectively initializes attacks by projecting prompts along compliance directions, increasing Attack Success Rate (ASR) and reducing computational overhead.
CRI performs well across multiple attacks, models, and datasets, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs.
The trade-off between the number of initializations (K) and their generalization properties affects performance, with intermediate K (e.g., 5) often optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gradient-based attacks may not generalize to other attack types.
Effectiveness depends on quality and diversity of fine-tuning set.
future_direction: Extending CRI to black-box settings
Integrating CRI with other attack improvements
Applying CRI to other types of attacks and defenses
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs respond to prompts with either compliance or refusal, each corresponding to distinct directions in the model's activation space. Recent works show that initializing attacks via self-transfer from other prompts significantly enhances their performance. However, the underlying mechanisms of these initializations remain unclear, and attacks utilize arbitrary or hand-picked initializations. This work presents that each gradient-based jailbreak attack and subsequent initialization gradually converge to a single compliance direction that suppresses refusal, thereby enabling an efficient transition from refusal to compliance. Based on this insight, we propose CRI, an initialization framework that aims to project unseen prompts further along compliance directions. We demonstrate our approach on multiple attacks, models, and datasets, achieving an increased attack success rate (ASR) and reduced computational overhead, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs. A reference implementation is available at: https://amit1221levi.github.io/CRI-Jailbreak-Init-LLMs-evaluation.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Hiding in Plain Text: Detecting Concealed Jailbreaks via Activation Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can we detect jailbreak prompts that preserve a harmful goal but manipulate its framing, by disentangling goal and framing representations in LLM activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-supervised framework for disentangling goal and framing representations in frozen LLM activations, leading to an effective jailbreak detection method (FrameShield) that improves detection across multiple LLM families with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: Semantic disentanglement of goal and framing in LLM activations enables effective detection of GPF jailbreaks and reveals layer-wise specialization of semantic factors, advancing both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed disentanglement framework (ReDAct) successfully separates goal and framing representations with controlled leakage.
FrameShield, which uses disentangled framing representations for anomaly detection, outperforms existing jailbreak detection methods across multiple LLM families.
Goal and framing signals concentrate at different layers in LLMs, providing interpretability insights.
The constructed GoalFrameBench dataset enables controlled study of goal-preserving framing attacks.
The method generalizes well to out-of-distribution goals.
papers.limitation:
ReDAct requires training on contrastive pairs, which depends on the quality and coverage of GoalFrameBench.
FrameShield’s detection performance may degrade if attackers devise framings that closely mimic benign patterns.
Our analysis focuses on goal and framing; other semantic factors could be relevant for safety.
future_direction: Extend the disentanglement framework to more than two factors.
Investigate the dynamics of semantic factor separation during training.
Explore applications beyond safety, such as controllable generation and bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that are fluent and semantically coherent, and therefore difficult to detect with standard heuristics. A particularly challenging failure mode occurs when an attacker tries to hide the malicious goal of their request by manipulating its framing to induce compliance. Because these attacks maintain malicious intent through a flexible presentation, defenses that rely on structural artifacts or goal-specific signatures can fail. Motivated by this, we introduce a self-supervised framework for disentangling semantic factor pairs in LLM activations at inference. We instantiate the framework for goal and framing and construct GoalFrameBench, a corpus of prompts with controlled goal and framing variations, which we use to train Representation Disentanglement on Activations (ReDAct) module to extract disentangled representations in a frozen LLM. We then propose FrameShield, an anomaly detector operating on the framing representations, which improves model-agnostic detection across multiple LLM families with minimal computational overhead. Theoretical guarantees for ReDAct and extensive empirical validations show that its disentanglement effectively powers FrameShield. Finally, we use disentanglement as an interpretability probe, revealing distinct profiles for goal and framing signals and positioning semantic disentanglement as a building block for both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: Interpretation Meets Safety: A Survey on Interpretation Methods and Tools for Improving LLM Safety
papers.core_contribution: This survey bridges the gap between LLM interpretation and safety, introducing a unified framework that connects safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancements they inform, and the tools that operationalize them.
papers.conclusion: This timely survey helps researchers and practitioners navigate key advancements for safer, more interpretable LLMs and outlines open challenges for future work.
papers.key_findings:
This is the first survey to bridge LLM interpretation and safety, providing a unified framework for summarizing safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancement strategies they inform, and the practical tools that operationalize them.
It introduces a novel taxonomy of LLM interpretation methods organized by LLM workflow stages: training process, input prompts, inference, and generation for self-reasoning.
The taxonomy connects interpretation methods to six safety enhancement strategies and four tool types, summarizing nearly 70 works at their intersections.
The survey distills open problems and challenges to guide future NLP research and raise awareness of unresolved safety issues.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) see wider real-world use, understanding and mitigating their unsafe behaviors is critical. Interpretation techniques can reveal causes of unsafe outputs and guide safety, but such connections with safety are often overlooked in prior surveys. We present the first survey that bridges this gap, introducing a unified framework that connects safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancements they inform, and the tools that operationalize them. Our novel taxonomy, organized by LLM workflow stages, summarizes nearly 70 works at their intersections. We conclude with open challenges and future directions. This timely survey helps researchers and practitioners navigate key advancements for safer, more interpretable LLMs.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: Targeting Alignment: Extracting Safety Classifiers of Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How accurate are candidate classifiers at approximating the safety classifier in benign and adversarial settings, and can they be used to jailbreak aligned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to extract surrogate classifiers from aligned LLMs, showing that these classifiers can approximate the safety classifier with high accuracy using only a subset of the model, and that attacking them leads to efficient and effective jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Extracting surrogate classifiers is an effective and efficient way to model and exploit vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs for jailbreaking attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Candidate classifiers achieve F1 score above 80% using as little as 20% of the model architecture.
Attacks on surrogate classifiers transfer to the LLM with high success, e.g., 70% ASR for Llama 2 with 50% of the model.
The approach reduces memory footprint and runtime compared to attacking the LLM directly.
Silhouette scores show separation between safe and unsafe inputs in internal decoders, supporting the existence of an embedded safety classifier.
Using misclassification as the adversarial objective removes constraints on the search space, improving attack efficacy.
papers.limitation:
The study uses temperature 0 for generation, leaving higher temperatures for future work.
The method is limited to structures starting from the first decoder, and exploring intermediate decoders is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring structures that isolate intermediate decoders
Applying the approach to other domains beyond safety
Studying the impact of temperature on attacks
papers.abstract: Alignment in large language models (LLMs) is used to enforce guidelines such as safety. Yet, alignment fails in the face of jailbreak attacks that modify inputs to induce unsafe outputs. In this paper, we introduce and evaluate a new technique for jailbreak attacks. We observe that alignment embeds a safety classifier in the LLM responsible for deciding between refusal and compliance, and seek to extract an approximation of this classifier: a surrogate classifier. To this end, we build candidate classifiers from subsets of the LLM. We first evaluate the degree to which candidate classifiers approximate the LLM's safety classifier in benign and adversarial settings. Then, we attack the candidates and measure how well the resulting adversarial inputs transfer to the LLM. Our evaluation shows that the best candidates achieve accurate agreement (an F1 score above 80%) using as little as 20% of the model architecture. Further, we find that attacks mounted on the surrogate classifiers can be transferred to the LLM with high success. For example, a surrogate using only 50% of the Llama 2 model achieved an attack success rate (ASR) of 70% with half the memory footprint and runtime -- a substantial improvement over attacking the LLM directly, where we only observed a 22% ASR. These results show that extracting surrogate classifiers is an effective and efficient means for modeling (and therein addressing) the vulnerability of aligned models to jailbreaking attacks. The code is available at https://github.com/jcnf0/targeting-alignment.

papers.title: Latent Fusion Jailbreak: Blending Harmful and Harmless Representations to Elicit Unsafe LLM Outputs
papers.research_question: Can latent representation manipulation achieve higher attack success rates and linguistic fluency than token-level optimization for jailbreaking LLMs? How does hidden state interpolation 'mask' malicious intent to circumvent refusal mechanisms? Can latent adversarial training mitigate these vulnerabilities without compromising general model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTFUSIONJAILBREAK (LFJ), a white-box attack that uses hidden state interpolation to blend harmful and benign representations in the latent space, achieving high attack success rates without detectable input artifacts. Also proposes a latent adversarial training defense that reduces the attack success rate by over 80%.
papers.conclusion: LFJ demonstrates that current safety alignments in LLMs are vulnerable to latent space attacks that blend harmful and benign representations. The proposed adversarial training defense effectively reduces the attack success rate while maintaining model utility.
papers.key_findings:
LFJ achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 94.01% across multiple models and benchmarks, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art discrete optimization and representation-based attacks.
Thematic similarity between harmful and benign queries is a critical factor for the success of the attack, with random pairing drastically reducing ASR.
Gradient-guided layer and token selection are essential components of the Hidden State Interpolation (HSI) mechanism, as ablations show significant drops in ASR when removed.
The proposed latent adversarial training defense reduces LFJ's ASR by over 80% while maintaining model utility on benign inputs.
Current safety alignments are vulnerable to latent space attacks that blend representations, highlighting a fundamental blindness to semantic superposition.
papers.limitation:
White-box dependency: The attack requires access to the model's internal weights and gradients, restricting application to open-source models.
Computational overhead: The iterative optimization and forward/backward passes increase inference latency compared to static prompt injection attacks.
Defense trade-offs: Adversarial training may incur an 'alignment tax', potentially degrading performance on complex benign instructions or increasing false refusals.
Scope of modality: The method is tailored for textual LLMs; extending it to multimodal models remains unexplored.
future_direction: Explore more disentangled representation editing methods to minimize the trade-offs in adversarial training defense.
Extend Hidden State Interpolation (HSI) to multimodal alignment for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing methods, primarily relying on discrete input optimization (e.g., GCG), often suffer from high computational costs and generate high-perplexity prompts that are easily blocked by simple filters. To overcome these limitations, we propose Latent Fusion Jailbreak (LFJ), a stealthy white-box attack that operates in the continuous latent space. Unlike previous approaches, LFJ constructs adversarial representations by mathematically fusing the hidden states of a harmful query with a thematically similar benign query, effectively masking malicious intent while retaining semantic drive. We further introduce a gradient-guided optimization strategy to balance attack success and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on Vicuna-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, Guanaco-7B, LLaMA-3-70B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct show that LFJ achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 94.01%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines like GCG and AutoDAN while avoiding detectable input artifacts. Furthermore, we identify that thematic similarity in the latent space is a critical vulnerability in current safety alignments. Finally, we propose a latent adversarial training defense that reduces LFJ's ASR by over 80% without compromising model utility.

papers.title: UpSafe$^\circ$C: Upcycling for Controllable Safety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety through a unified framework that balances safety, utility, and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes UPSAFE°C, a safety-aware upcycling framework that identifies safety-critical layers, converts them into a sparse MoE structure with a soft guardrail router, and introduces a safety temperature for inference-time control, achieving robust safety improvements while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: UPSAFE°C offers a novel direction for LLM safety by shifting from static alignment toward dynamic, modular, and inference-aware control, achieving a favorable balance between safety and utility.
papers.key_findings:
UPSAFE°C significantly enhances safety performance on benchmarks like JBB, StrongReject, WildChat, and WildJailbreak, often reaching 100% safety rates.
The method maintains or improves general capabilities on tasks like HumanEval, MMLU, and Math-500 compared to baselines.
The safety temperature mechanism provides fine-grained inference-time control, allowing dynamic adjustment of the safety-utility trade-off and achieving Pareto-optimal frontiers.
The router acts as an effective soft guardrail, selectively activating safety experts for harmful inputs and the general expert for benign inputs.
Ablation studies show the importance of the safety-critical layer scan, the two-stage training strategy, and a moderate number of safety experts for optimal performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of tasks, but remain vulnerable to safety risks such as harmful content generation and jailbreak attacks. Existing safety techniques -- including external guardrails, inference-time guidance, and post-training alignment -- each face limitations in balancing safety, utility, and controllability. In this work, we propose UpSafe$^\circ$C, a unified framework for enhancing LLM safety through safety-aware upcycling. Our approach first identifies safety-critical layers and upcycles them into a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure, where the router acts as a soft guardrail that selectively activates original MLPs and added safety experts. We further introduce a two-stage SFT strategy to strengthen safety discrimination while preserving general capabilities. To enable flexible control at inference time, we introduce a safety temperature mechanism, allowing dynamic adjustment of the trade-off between safety and utility. Experiments across multiple benchmarks, base model, and model scales demonstrate that UpSafe$^\circ$C achieves robust safety improvements against harmful and jailbreak inputs, while maintaining competitive performance on general tasks. Moreover, analysis shows that safety temperature provides fine-grained inference-time control that achieves the Pareto-optimal frontier between utility and safety. Our results highlight a new direction for LLM safety: moving from static alignment toward dynamic, modular, and inference-aware control.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: False Sense of Security: Why Probing-based Malicious Input Detection Fails to Generalize
papers.research_question: Do probing classifiers for LLM safety detection learn semantic harmfulness or rely on superficial patterns?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that probing classifiers for LLM safety detection rely on superficial patterns like instructional formats and trigger words, rather than semantic understanding of harmfulness, leading to poor out-of-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current probing-based safety detection methods provide a false sense of security by relying on spurious correlations, and calls for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fail dramatically on out-of-distribution data.
Simple n-gram methods achieve comparable performance to probing classifiers, suggesting reliance on surface-level patterns.
Classifiers perform poorly on semantically cleaned datasets where harmful content is replaced with benign alternatives.
Probing classifiers depend on instructional patterns and trigger words rather than semantic harmfulness.
LLMs themselves possess zero-shot safety classification ability, but probing classifiers cannot leverage this effectively.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets, which may not generalize to other languages and cultural contexts.
Analysis is restricted to decoder-only transformer models, leaving other architectures unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can comply with harmful instructions, raising serious safety concerns despite their impressive capabilities. Recent work has leveraged probing-based approaches to study the separability of malicious and benign inputs in LLMs' internal representations, and researchers have proposed using such probing methods for safety detection. We systematically re-examine this paradigm. Motivated by poor out-of-distribution performance, we hypothesize that probes learn superficial patterns rather than semantic harmfulness. Through controlled experiments, we confirm this hypothesis and identify the specific patterns learned: instructional patterns and trigger words. Our investigation follows a systematic approach, progressing from demonstrating comparable performance of simple n-gram methods, to controlled experiments with semantically cleaned datasets, to detailed analysis of pattern dependencies. These results reveal a false sense of security around current probing-based approaches and highlight the need to redesign both models and evaluation protocols, for which we provide further discussions in the hope of suggesting responsible further research in this direction. We have open-sourced the project at https://github.com/WangCheng0116/Why-Probe-Fails.

papers.title: SCANS: Mitigating the Exaggerated Safety for LLMs via Safety-Conscious Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the exaggerated safety issue in safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) that cause them to refuse benign queries, without compromising their defense against harmful queries?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SCANS, a training-free activation steering method that extracts refusal steering vectors from model hidden states and steers activations in safety-critical layers to reduce false refusals on benign queries while maintaining defense against harmful ones.
papers.conclusion: SCANS effectively mitigates exaggerated safety in aligned LLMs via activation steering in safety-critical layers, achieving a better balance between safety and helpfulness without significantly compromising model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SCANS significantly reduces false refusal rates on safe queries (e.g., by 24.7% on XSTest and 26.3% on OKTest on average) without compromising adequate safety against harmful queries.
Refusal steering vectors extracted from middle layers promote refusal tokens; steering these vectors reduces false refusal behavior.
A similarity-based classification method using hidden state transition effectively distinguishes harmful from benign queries.
SCANS maintains general model capabilities (perplexity, summarization, QA) with minimal inference overhead.
Larger models (13B) are more robust to the steering intervention than smaller models (7B).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is indispensable for Large language models (LLMs) to defend threats from malicious instructions. However, recent researches reveal safety-aligned LLMs tend to reject benign queries due to the exaggerated safety issue, limiting their helpfulness. In this paper, we propose a Safety-Conscious Activation Steering (SCANS) method to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned LLMs. First, SCANS extracts the refusal steering vectors within the activation space and utilizes vocabulary projection to anchor some specific safety-critical layers which influence model refusal behavior. Second, by tracking the hidden state transition, SCANS identifies the steering direction and steers the model behavior accordingly, achieving a balance between exaggerated safety and adequate safety. Experiments show that SCANS achieves new state-of-the-art performance on XSTest and OKTest benchmarks, without impairing their defense capability against harmful queries and maintaining almost unchanged model capability.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Antidote: Post-fine-tuning Safety Alignment for Large Language Models against Harmful Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: Is there a defense that can be less sensitive to the hyper-parameters of the fine-tuning stage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Antidote, a post-fine-tuning defense that prunes harmful weights to recover model safety, which is agnostic to fine-tuning hyper-parameters and reduces harmful score while maintaining downstream task accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Antidote provides an effective post-fine-tuning safety alignment solution that mitigates harmful fine-tuning attacks by pruning harmful parameters, addressing the hyper-parameter sensitivity of prior defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Existing alignment-stage and fine-tuning-stage defenses are highly sensitive to fine-tuning hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs), a weakness termed the hyper-parameter sensitivity issue.
Antidote, a one-shot pruning method applied after fine-tuning, effectively reduces harmful scores across various harmful data ratios and fine-tuning settings.
Antidote maintains downstream task accuracy close to the undefended baseline while significantly improving safety.
The method generalizes across different model architectures (Llama2, Mistral, Gemma) and is compatible with stronger safety alignment datasets.
Antidote introduces minimal system overhead compared to other defense methods, mainly from calculating the Wanda score.
papers.limitation: Requires access to a separate harmful dataset (re-alignment dataset) for calculating the pruning mask.
future_direction: Exploring model acceleration benefits from the pruning step.
Extending the method to more advanced models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Safety aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to harmful fine-tuning attacks -- a few harmful data mixed in the fine-tuning dataset can break the LLMs's safety alignment. While several defenses have been proposed, our evaluation shows that existing defenses fail \textit{when some specific training hyper-parameters are chosen} -- a large learning rate or a large number of training epochs in the fine-tuning stage can easily invalidate the defense. To this end, we propose Antidote, a post-fine-tuning stage solution, which remains \textbf{\textit{agnostic to the training hyper-parameters in the fine-tuning stage}}. Antidote relies on the philosophy that by removing the harmful parameters, the harmful model can be recovered from the harmful behaviors, regardless of how those harmful parameters are formed in the fine-tuning stage. With this philosophy, we introduce a one-shot pruning stage after harmful fine-tuning to remove the harmful weights that are responsible for the generation of harmful content. Despite its embarrassing simplicity, empirical results show that Antidote can reduce harmful score while maintaining accuracy on downstream tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/git-disl/Antidote.

papers.title: Making Harmful Behaviors Unlearnable for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a controllable fine-tuning framework using 'security vectors' (additional parameters) to make harmful behaviors unlearnable during training, preventing LLMs from learning from harmful data while preserving their ability to learn other tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework with security vectors effectively prevents LLMs from learning harmful behaviors during fine-tuning, reducing security risks and enabling safer model customization.
papers.key_findings:
Security vectors trained on 100 harmful samples can prevent an LLM from learning harmful behaviors from 1000 harmful examples.
The method prevents learning from both explicit and implicit harmful data, maintaining safety levels comparable to the original aligned model.
Fine-tuning with security vectors does not impair the model's ability to learn new, benign tasks (e.g., ProfileQA).
The approach is robust across different training epochs and learning rates, except when the fine-tuning learning rate is much higher than that used to generate the security vectors.
Security vectors can be deactivated during inference, restoring the model's normal, safe behavior.
papers.limitation:
The security vectors may lose effectiveness if the fine-tuning learning rate is significantly higher (e.g., 5e-3) than the rate used to generate them (1e-3).
Excessive training epochs on harmful data may impair the model's reasoning ability (e.g., on GSM), though the cause is not fully determined.
future_direction: Design experiments to ascertain the cause of the drop in reasoning ability (GSM) when fine-tuning on harmful data.
Investigate the robust instruction-following capability observed when fine-tuning with security vectors over many epochs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose AI assistants in various domains. To meet the requirements of different applications, LLMs are often customized by further fine-tuning. However, the powerful learning ability of LLMs not only enables them to acquire new tasks but also makes them susceptible to learning undesired behaviors. For example, even safety-aligned LLMs can be easily fine-tuned into harmful assistants as the fine-tuning data often contains implicit or explicit harmful content. Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors? This paper proposes a controllable training framework that makes harmful behaviors unlearnable during the fine-tuning process. Specifically, we introduce ``security vectors'', a few new parameters that can be separated from the LLM, to ensure LLM's responses are consistent with the harmful behavior. Security vectors are activated during fine-tuning, the consistent behavior makes LLM believe that such behavior has already been learned, there is no need to further optimize for harmful data. During inference, we can deactivate security vectors to restore the LLM's normal behavior. The experimental results show that the security vectors generated by 100 harmful samples are enough to prevent LLM from learning 1000 harmful samples, while preserving the ability to learn other useful information.

papers.title: Learning Safety Constraints for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we learn and enforce safety constraints in large language models via a geometric polytope in the model's representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SaP, a geometric framework that learns safety constraints as a polytope in the LLM's representation space, enabling post-hoc safety steering and interpretable insights into safety concepts.
papers.conclusion: The geometric perspective of safety constraints offers a promising framework for aligning and controlling model behaviors, though further research is needed for theoretical foundations and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
SaP effectively defends against adversarial attacks while preserving model capabilities on standard benchmarks.
The learned polytope facets naturally correspond to different semantic safety concepts (e.g., violence, misinformation).
The concept encoder reduces polysemanticity in the learned features, improving interpretability and defense performance.
SaP's geometric approach provides a more structured and effective safety model compared to MLP-based classifiers.
The method operates post-hoc without model fine-tuning, preserving original model weights.
papers.limitation:
The heuristic facet assignment algorithm limits overall performance.
Under many attacks, specifically for the Ministral-8B model, SaP can induce semantically incoherent outputs.
Lacks a rigorous theoretical understanding and formal guarantees for safety in large-scale models.
future_direction: Further disentangling semantic understandings across polytope edges, possibly using mechanistic interpretability or non-linear geometric representations.
Improving SaP's performance in adversarial robustness and broad capability domains.
Adapting theoretical sample complexity bounds for learning polytopes to the context of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools but pose significant safety risks through harmful outputs and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We propose SaP, short for Safety Polytope, a geometric approach to LLM safety that learns and enforces multiple safety constraints directly in the model's representation space. We develop a framework that identifies safe and unsafe regions via the polytope's facets, enabling both detection and correction of unsafe outputs through geometric steering. Unlike existing approaches that modify model weights, SaP operates post-hoc in the representation space, preserving model capabilities while enforcing safety constraints. Experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that our method can effectively detect unethical inputs, reduce adversarial attack success rates while maintaining performance on standard tasks, thus highlighting the importance of having an explicit geometric model for safety. Analysis of the learned polytope facets reveals emergence of specialization in detecting different semantic notions of safety, providing interpretable insights into how safety is captured in LLMs' representation space.

papers.title: X-Boundary: Establishing Exact Safety Boundary to Shield LLMs from Multi-Turn Jailbreaks without Compromising Usability
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid development of safety alignment techniques for LLMs, defending against multi-turn jailbreaks is still a challenging task. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive comparison, revealing that some existing defense methods can improve the robustness of LLMs against multi-turn jailbreaks but compromise usability, i.e., reducing general capabilities or causing the over-refusal problem. From the perspective of mechanism interpretability of LLMs, we discover that these methods fail to establish a boundary that exactly distinguishes safe and harmful feature representations. Therefore, boundary-safe representations close to harmful representations are inevitably disrupted, leading to a decline in usability. To address this issue, we propose X-Boundary to push harmful representations away from boundary-safe representations and obtain an exact distinction boundary. In this way, harmful representations can be precisely erased without disrupting safe ones. Experimental results show that X-Boundary achieves state-of-the-art defense performance against multi-turn jailbreaks, while reducing the over-refusal rate by about 20% and maintaining nearly complete general capability. Furthermore, we theoretically prove and empirically verify that X-Boundary can accelerate the convergence process during training. Please see our code at: https://github.com/AI45Lab/X-Boundary.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: JPU: Bridging Jailbreak Defense and Unlearning via On-Policy Path Rectification
papers.research_question: What causes the failure of existing unlearning defenses against jailbreak attacks, and how can dynamic jailbreak paths be rectified to enhance defense?
papers.core_contribution: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples, significantly enhancing jailbreak resistance while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths via on-policy rectification, achieving superior defense performance against diverse jailbreak attacks while preserving general utility.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks activate non-erased parameters in intermediate layers, causing existing unlearning defenses to fail.
Dynamic jailbreak paths persist in erased LLMs and constitute the fundamental defense gap.
JPU effectively rectifies these paths, reducing attack success rate across diverse jailbreak attacks.
